name: LoadingBarUI
src_typeComment: Plug-and-play loading bar. HOW REAL LOADING PROGRESS ACTUALLY WORKS (read this before wiring anything — there is no single "loading progress" number Unity computes for you, only two real sources, and this component can be driven by either):  1) Unity's own AsyncOperation.progress — returned by SceneManager.LoadSceneAsync, AssetBundle. LoadFromFileAsync, Resources.UnloadUnusedAssets, Addressables, etc. The operation itself reports how far along it is; you just poll operation.progress every frame. Call Bind(operation) and this component does that polling for you automatically. GOTCHA specific to scene loads: SceneManager.LoadSceneAsync's progress caps at 0.9 and sits there until you explicitly set operation.allowSceneActivation = true — Unity deliberately holds back the last 10% so the new scene doesn't activate the instant loading finishes (giving you a chance to show "Press any key" or wait for a minimum display time first, the same thing Toolkit.UI. AsyncSceneLoader does). Use BindSceneLoad(operation) instead of Bind() for a scene-load operation — it remaps 0..0.9 -> 0..1 automatically so the bar still reaches a clean 100%.  2) A manually computed fraction — for anything that ISN'T a Unity AsyncOperation at all (a custom boot sequence, a multi-step save file, a fake splash-screen delay). YOU compute completedSteps / totalSteps (or bytesDownloaded / totalBytes, etc.) yourself and call SetProgress(that value) whenever it changes. SimulateProgress() below is a ready-made example of exactly this pattern with nothing real behind it — handy for building/testing a loading screen before the real work it represents exists yet.  Either way, the DISPLAYED bar doesn't snap straight to a new value — it smoothly chases it (smoothSpeed) instead. Real progress sources often jump in large, uneven steps (one asset bundle finishing, one big step out of ten completing), and a bar that visibly teleports looks broken even though the underlying number was completely accurate — smoothing is purely cosmetic, layered on top of the real progress.

src_serialized.name: slider
src_serialized.tooltip: Auto-found on this GameObject or its children if left empty. Expects the default 0..1 min/max range.

src_serialized.name: percentText
src_serialized.tooltip: Optional — shows the percentage as text, e.g. "45%". Leave empty if not needed.

src_serialized.name: smoothSpeed
src_serialized.tooltip: How fast the visible bar chases the real target progress, in fraction-per-second. Higher = snappier/closer to the raw value, lower = smoother but laggier.

src_members.sig: public void Bind(AsyncOperation operation) => BindInternal(operation, remap: false)
src_members.name: Bind
src_members.comment: Drives this bar from a real Unity AsyncOperation that does NOT have the scene-load 0.9 cap (an AssetBundle load, Resources.UnloadUnusedAssets, etc.) — polled automatically every frame from here on, no manual SetProgress calls needed.

src_members.sig: public void BindSceneLoad(AsyncOperation sceneLoadOperation) => BindInternal(sceneLoadOperation, remap: true)
src_members.name: BindSceneLoad
src_members.comment: Same as Bind(), but for the specific case of SceneManager.LoadSceneAsync — remaps its 0..0.9 ceiling onto a clean 0..1 so the bar actually reaches 100% instead of visibly stalling at 90%. See the class header for why that cap exists.

src_members.name: SetProgress
src_members.comment: For anything that ISN'T backed by a real AsyncOperation — call this yourself with completedSteps / totalSteps (or any other real 0..1 fraction) each time it changes.

src_members.sig: public void SimulateProgress(float duration, Action onComplete = null)
src_members.name: SimulateProgress
src_members.comment: A fake, time-based progress fill with NO real work behind it — useful for prototyping a loading screen's look before the thing it represents exists yet. Swap this for Bind()/BindSceneLoad() or your own SetProgress() calls once there's something real to track — this is a placeholder, not a technique to ship with.
